essentials.heading: S3 storage classes & retrieval trade-offs
essentials.body:
**What.** S3 exposes a spectrum of object storage classes that trade storage price against retrieval latency and per-GB retrieval fees. The hot end is `Standard`; the cold end is `Glacier Deep Archive`.

**Why.** Match each object's access pattern to the cheapest class that still meets latency and SLA needs, instead of paying Standard prices for cold data.

**How.** **Standard** (frequent, ms, no retrieval fee), **Intelligent-Tiering** (auto-moves, small monitoring fee, no retrieval charges), **Standard-IA** (cheaper storage + retrieval fee, multi-AZ), **One Zone-IA** (~20% cheaper, single AZ), **Glacier Instant** (ms but archive-priced), **Glacier Flexible** (min–hrs: Expedited 1–5 min, Standard 3–5 h, Bulk 5–12 h), **Glacier Deep Archive** (12–48 h, cheapest).

**Exam.** All classes give **11 9s durability**; only One Zone-IA lacks multi-AZ. Minimum storage durations: **IA 30 d**, **Glacier Instant/Flexible 90 d**, **Deep Archive 180 d** — deleting earlier still bills the floor. Intelligent-Tiering when access is unknown; avoid it for tiny objects (< 128 KB are not tiered). Rare access with a tolerant (up to 24 h) retrieval time is Glacier territory: a lifecycle rule can transition objects after 0 days. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA cost more (One Zone-IA is single-AZ, not for financial records) and FSx is not an archive.

diagram.caption: S3 storage classes along the access-frequency spectrum: hotter classes cost more to store with instant access; colder classes are cheaper but charge retrieval fees and take longer.

essentials.heading: Lifecycle policies & cost optimization
essentials.body:
**What.** Lifecycle configuration is a bucket-level rule set that automates moving objects between storage classes (`Transition`) and deleting them (`Expiration`) based on age, prefix, or tag.

**Why.** It removes the need for hand-rolled cron jobs and stops paying Standard prices for data that has gone cold or for orphaned versions and multipart parts.

**How.** A typical rule cascades **Standard → Standard-IA at 30 d → Glacier at 90 d → Deep Archive at 365 d**, then expires noncurrent versions. Use `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` to bound versioning cost and `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` to clean orphaned parts. **Storage Lens** and **S3 Inventory** identify what to transition.

**Exam.** Transitions cannot bypass the **minimum-duration floors** (IA 30 d, Glacier 90 d, Deep Archive 180 d) — and you still pay the floor if you delete early. For unknown/changing access patterns prefer **Intelligent-Tiering** over hand-tuned rules; small objects move cheaper if you skip the IA step.

essentials.heading: Durability, availability, versioning & MFA delete
essentials.body:
**What.** S3 stores objects redundantly across multiple devices and AZs and can keep every prior version of a key. Versioning plus MFA Delete forms the data-protection baseline.

**Why.** Defends against accidental overwrites, application bugs, and malicious deletes — including ransomware-style destruction of older copies.

**How.** Standard, IA, Glacier and Intelligent-Tiering replicate across ≥3 AZs; only **One Zone-IA** lives in a single AZ. **Versioning** is bucket-wide: a `DELETE` adds a delete marker instead of erasing data; once enabled it can only be **suspended**, never disabled. **MFA Delete** can only be toggled by the **root account via CLI** and requires an MFA code to permanently delete versions or suspend versioning.

**Exam.** Memorize **11 9s durability (99.999999999%)** and Standard's **99.99% availability SLA**. Versioning is a prerequisite for **CRR/SRR**. MFA Delete is root-only and cannot be enabled via the console. **Object Lock (WORM)** requires versioning: **compliance mode** — no one, not even root, can delete a version or shorten retention ("strict regulatory", "immutable"); **governance mode** — users with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` can override (testing, internal policy); **legal hold** — no expiry until removed. Classic combo: versioning + Object Lock compliance + lifecycle to Glacier Deep Archive.

essentials.heading: S3 security: policies, BPA, encryption, presigned URLs
essentials.body:
**What.** S3 layers access control (BPA, bucket policies, IAM, ACLs), encryption at rest (SSE variants and client-side), and short-lived signed access (presigned URLs).

**Why.** Prevents accidental public exposure, satisfies regulatory encryption and audit requirements, and lets you share private objects without distributing AWS credentials.

**How.** **Block Public Access (BPA)** is on by default and overrides policies/ACLs. Encrypt with **SSE-S3** (AES-256, default), **SSE-KMS** (KMS CMK, CloudTrail audit + cross-account via key policy; enable **S3 Bucket Keys** to cut KMS request cost), **DSSE-KMS** (dual-layer), or **SSE-C** (customer-supplied key on every request). **Presigned URLs** grant temporary `GET`/`PUT` access.

**Exam.** **BPA is on by default** — disabling it is a frequent trap. A presigned URL is bounded by the **signer's permissions** and its expiry; revoking IAM perms invalidates it. SSE-KMS is required when the question demands a per-decrypt CloudTrail audit trail. Request headers: SSE-S3 → `x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256`; SSE-KMS → same header with `aws:kms` (+ `x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id`); **SSE-C** → `x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-algorithm`, `-customer-key`, `-customer-key-MD5` on every PUT/GET. A bucket policy can deny `PutObject` without the expected header (the least-effort way to guarantee that no unencrypted object is ever uploaded; an SCP targets accounts/OUs, not one bucket). **SSE-S3** keys are managed and rotated automatically by AWS (nothing to operate), whereas a customer-managed KMS key adds rotation settings to manage and Object Lock has nothing to do with key rotation. **Encrypt BEFORE upload** → **client-side encryption** with a **KMS key** or your own **client-side master key** (you manage the keys); every SSE variant encrypts only after S3 receives the data. **HIPAA-style "S3 data must be encrypted":** use **server-side encryption with AES-256** and/or **client-side encryption** with your own keys; S3 has **no AES-128** SSE, and EBS encryption or encrypted EBS snapshots are different storage and do not protect S3 objects.

diagram.caption: S3 encryption options compared: SSE-KMS and DSSE-KMS provide CloudTrail audit and cross-account access via the key policy; SSE-C and client-side encryption keep keys outside AWS.

essentials.heading: Replication, Transfer Acceleration & multipart upload
essentials.body:
**What.** S3 ships objects between buckets asynchronously (CRR/SRR), speeds long-distance uploads (Transfer Acceleration), and chunks big objects (multipart upload) for throughput and resume.

**Why.** Solves disaster recovery, compliance residency, log aggregation, fast global ingest, and reliable upload of multi-gigabyte objects over flaky networks.

**How.** **CRR** (cross-region: DR, latency, compliance) and **SRR** (same-region: log aggregation, account isolation) both require **versioning on source and destination** plus an **IAM role**. **Transfer Acceleration** routes uploads through **CloudFront edge** locations. **Multipart upload** is recommended for objects > 100 MB and required > 5 GB; abort incomplete parts via lifecycle.

**Exam.** Replication is **not retroactive** — existing objects need **S3 Batch Replication**. Prefixes scale to **3,500 PUT / 5,500 GET req/s each**, so shard keys for high throughput. Use a **Gateway Endpoint for S3** to avoid NAT data charges from a private subnet. **Transfer Acceleration vs CloudFront:** TA speeds up each individual transfer over the AWS backbone (best for long-distance *uploads*) but caches nothing; **Region failure:** S3 is already multi-AZ, so survive a Region outage with **Cross-Region Replication** (versioning on both buckets), not a lifecycle rule, an EBS copy or cross-account bucket access; when many clients worldwide repeatedly *download* the same objects, put **CloudFront** in front of the bucket (edge cache + signed URLs).

essentials.heading: EBS volume types & snapshots
essentials.body:
**What.** EBS is network-attached block storage that lives in a **single AZ** and attaches to one EC2 instance (Multi-Attach is io1/io2 only, same-AZ). Volumes come in SSD and HDD families.

**Why.** Provides persistent, low-latency block devices for boot volumes, databases, and throughput-heavy log/batch workloads — and lets you back them up cheaply via snapshots.

**How.** **gp3** (general SSD, baseline 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s, provision up to 16,000 IOPS / 1,000 MB/s independent of size). **io2 / io2 Block Express** (highest IOPS, sub-ms, 99.999% durability, Multi-Attach). **st1** (throughput HDD, sequential big data). **sc1** (cold HDD, cheapest). **Snapshots** are incremental, stored in S3, **region-scoped** — copy across regions for DR.

**Exam.** EBS is **single-AZ**: AZ failure means restore from snapshot. KMS-encrypted volumes produce encrypted snapshots; snapshots can be shared but encrypted ones need a shared CMK. gp3 usually beats gp2 on price/perf. **Automating snapshots:** **Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM)** — free, tag-based policies that create, retain and delete EBS snapshots/AMIs on a schedule — is the fastest, cheapest answer for "automated EBS backups"; choose **AWS Backup** when the stem spans many services/accounts or needs Vault Lock/compliance; a cron job calling `create-snapshot` is never the "simple to maintain" answer. **Type-description traps:** **Provisioned IOPS (io1/io2)** = consistent low latency for I/O-intensive large relational/NoSQL databases; **Magnetic (standard)** = lowest cost per GB for rarely accessed data; **gp3** = general purpose (boot, dev/test, small-medium DBs), no Multi-Attach and never multi-AZ; 'Spot volumes' and 'SR-IOV volumes' do not exist (Spot is a purchase model, SR-IOV is enhanced networking). **EBS encryption** at rest uses **KMS** keys, either the **AWS managed key** or your **own customer managed key** (symmetric only) for volumes, boot volumes and snapshots; CloudHSM passwords, S3 SSE and ACM certificates are not part of it. **Valid EBS facts:** persists independently of the instance, supports live **Elastic Volumes** changes (type, size, IOPS) without downtime, is replicated only **within its AZ**, attaches only to instances in the **same AZ**, and snapshots are stored in **S3** (not RDS). **Encrypted volume behavior:** snapshots of an encrypted volume are **automatically encrypted**, volumes restored from an encrypted snapshot are **encrypted**, and **all data moving between the volume and the instance is encrypted** (in transit as well as at rest).

diagram.caption: EBS volume types plotted against cost and performance: HDD st1/sc1 for sequential/cold workloads, gp3 as the default SSD, io2 Block Express for highest IOPS, durability and Multi-Attach.

essentials.heading: EFS vs FSx vs instance store
essentials.body:
**What.** A family of shared and local file/block options beyond EBS: **EFS** (managed NFS), **FSx** (managed Windows/Lustre/ONTAP/OpenZFS file systems), and **instance store** (host-local ephemeral disks).

**Why.** EBS attaches to one instance in one AZ; real workloads also need multi-instance shared file systems, Windows SMB shares, HPC/ML throughput, and ultra-fast scratch space.

**How.** **EFS** = Linux NFS, multi-AZ, elastic, POSIX, mountable by many EC2/containers; lifecycle tiers cold files to **EFS-IA**. **FSx for Windows** = SMB + AD. **FSx for Lustre** = HPC/ML, hundreds of GB/s, can lazy-load from S3. **FSx for NetApp ONTAP / OpenZFS** for multi-protocol and migration. **Instance store** = NVMe attached to the host, ephemeral.

**Exam.** **EFS = Linux NFS**; FSx for Windows = SMB. **FSx Lustre** is the HPC/ML answer (S3-linked training data). **Instance store data is lost on stop/terminate** and host failure — caches/scratch only. **EFS for many containers:** hundreds of ECS tasks hitting one shared file system constantly = **EFS** mounted in the task definition; for sustained high throughput pick **Provisioned Throughput** (Bursting credits scale with stored size and run out under constant load) and **Max I/O** performance mode for massive parallelism (performance mode is fixed at creation). FSx for Windows is SMB/Windows, DynamoDB cannot be mounted.

essentials.heading: Storage Gateway types
essentials.body:
**What.** AWS Storage Gateway is a hybrid appliance (VM or hardware) that presents AWS storage to on-prem servers via standard protocols: NFS/SMB, iSCSI, or iSCSI-VTL.

**Why.** Lets existing on-prem applications, backup software, and tape libraries consume S3/Glacier/FSx without rewriting — useful for cloud migration, tiered storage, and DR.

**How.** **S3 File Gateway** exposes S3 buckets as NFS/SMB shares. **FSx File Gateway** caches FSx for Windows locally for low-latency branch access. **Volume Gateway** serves iSCSI block volumes: *Cached* keeps hot data on-prem with primary in S3, *Stored* keeps everything local and backs up to S3 as EBS snapshots. **Tape Gateway** is a VTL backing to S3/Glacier/Deep Archive.

**Exam.** Map by protocol: **NFS/SMB → File Gateway**, **iSCSI block → Volume Gateway**, **iSCSI VTL → Tape Gateway**. Tape Gateway is the standard answer for replacing physical tape libraries and shipping to Deep Archive. On-prem backups over **standard file protocols** stored durably in S3 → **File Gateway** (Volume Gateway data isn't reachable through the S3 API; DataSync is a transfer tool, EBS attaches only to EC2).

labs.title: Bucket with versioning + lifecycle to Glacier
labs.intro: Create a bucket, enable **versioning**, and add a **lifecycle rule** transitioning objects to Glacier and expiring old noncurrent versions for cost savings.
labs.pulumi:
import pulumi
import pulumi_aws as aws

bucket = aws.s3.BucketV2("saa-lab", bucket="my-saa-lab-bucket")

aws.s3.BucketVersioningV2(
    "saa-lab-versioning",
    bucket=bucket.id,
    versioning_configuration={"status": "Enabled"},
)

aws.s3.BucketLifecycleConfigurationV2(
    "saa-lab-lifecycle",
    bucket=bucket.id,
    rules=[{
        "id": "archive-then-expire",
        "status": "Enabled",
        "filter": {"prefix": ""},
        "transitions": [
            {"days": 30, "storage_class": "STANDARD_IA"},
            {"days": 90, "storage_class": "GLACIER"},
        ],
        "noncurrent_version_expiration": {"noncurrent_days": 60},
        "abort_incomplete_multipart_upload": {"days_after_initiation": 7},
    }],
)

pulumi.export("bucket_name", bucket.bucket)
labs.note: **Cleanup**: delete all object versions and delete markers first (`aws s3api delete-objects` per version) then `aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket my-saa-lab-bucket`, or `pulumi destroy`. A versioned bucket cannot be deleted while it contains versions.

labs.title: Enable default SSE-KMS encryption + Block Public Access
labs.intro: Set **default encryption with SSE-KMS** (using a Bucket Key to reduce KMS costs) and confirm **Block Public Access** is fully on.
labs.note: **Cleanup**: encryption/BPA config is removed automatically when the bucket is deleted, or run `pulumi destroy`. Using the AWS-managed `alias/aws/s3` key incurs no extra KMS key charge; a customer-managed key would.

questions.stem: A company stores log files in S3. Logs are read heavily for 30 days, occasionally for the next 60 days, and almost never afterward but must be kept 7 years for compliance with retrieval allowed within 12 hours. Which lifecycle minimizes cost?
options: Standard for 30 days, transition to Standard-IA at 30 days, then to Glacier Deep Archive at 90 days
Intelligent-Tiering for the full 7 years
Standard-IA immediately, then One Zone-IA after 90 days
Keep everything in S3 Standard for 7 years
questions.explanation: Correct: hot reads stay in Standard, occasional access fits Standard-IA, and rarely-accessed long-term data with a 12-hour retrieval tolerance is cheapest in Glacier Deep Archive. Keeping all in Standard wastes money on cold data. One Zone-IA risks data loss on AZ failure and is unsuitable for compliance retention; it also is not cheaper than Deep Archive for archival. Intelligent-Tiering avoids retrieval fees but its archive tiers and monitoring fee cost more than an explicit transition to Deep Archive when the access pattern is known.

questions.stem: A web app must let users download private S3 objects for a limited time without exposing the bucket publicly and without distributing AWS credentials. What should you use?
options: Generate presigned URLs with a short expiration
Disable Block Public Access and add a public-read bucket policy
Share an IAM user's access keys with the client app
Enable static website hosting on the bucket
questions.explanation: Correct: presigned URLs grant time-limited access using the signer's permissions, keeping the bucket private and credentials secret. Disabling BPA with public-read exposes all objects publicly. Sharing IAM access keys is a major security risk and violates least privilege. Static website hosting also requires public access and does not provide time-limited private access.

questions.stem: Several hundred Linux EC2 instances across multiple AZs need to read and write the same set of files concurrently with POSIX semantics. Which storage service fits best?
options: EC2 instance store
Amazon EFS
Amazon EBS gp3 volume attached to each instance
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
questions.explanation: Correct: EFS is a managed, multi-AZ NFS file system that many Linux instances can mount and share simultaneously with POSIX semantics. EBS is single-AZ and (except io1/io2 Multi-Attach within one AZ) attaches to one instance, so it can't be shared across AZs. FSx for Windows uses SMB and targets Windows workloads. Instance store is ephemeral, host-local, and not shareable.

questions.stem: A high-performance computing ML training job needs a file system delivering hundreds of GB/s throughput and sub-millisecond latency, with the ability to load training data directly from an S3 bucket. Which service should you choose?
options: Amazon EFS with Max I/O mode
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket
S3 with Transfer Acceleration
questions.explanation: Correct: FSx for Lustre is purpose-built for HPC/ML with very high throughput and low latency, and can be linked to an S3 bucket to lazily load and write back data. EFS scales well but does not match Lustre's throughput/latency for HPC. FSx for Windows is an SMB Windows file server, not an HPC file system. Transfer Acceleration only speeds S3 uploads over distance; it is not a mountable high-performance file system.

questions.stem: An application's S3 access pattern is unpredictable: some objects are read often, others go cold for months, and the pattern changes over time. The team wants to avoid per-object analysis and retrieval-fee surprises. Which storage class is most appropriate?
options: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Standard-IA
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 One Zone-IA
questions.explanation: Correct: Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage with no retrieval fees, ideal for unknown or changing patterns. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA charge retrieval fees and have 30-day minimums, penalizing frequently re-read objects, and One Zone-IA also sacrifices AZ redundancy. Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires restore operations of minutes to hours, unacceptable for objects that may be read often.

questions.stem: A regulated workload requires encryption at rest with an auditable trail of every key use and fine-grained control over who can decrypt objects, including cross-account access. Which S3 encryption option meets this best?
options: Client-side encryption with a hardcoded application key
SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key
SSE-S3 (Amazon S3-managed keys)
SSE-C (customer-provided keys)
questions.explanation: Correct: SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key logs every decrypt call in CloudTrail and lets you control access via the key policy, including cross-account grants. SSE-S3 gives no per-request audit trail or key-level access control. SSE-C requires you to manage and transmit keys on every request with no KMS audit. A hardcoded application key is insecure and unmanaged. Enable S3 Bucket Keys to reduce KMS costs.

questions.stem: An application running on EC2 needs a single block volume providing a consistent 16,000 IOPS and 500 MB/s throughput for a self-managed database, while keeping cost as low as possible. Which EBS configuration is best? (Choose two)
options: Use a gp3 volume and provision the required IOPS and throughput
Use an sc1 (cold HDD) volume for lowest cost
Provision IOPS/throughput independently of the volume's storage size
Use an st1 (throughput-optimized HDD) volume
questions.explanation: Correct: gp3 lets you provision IOPS (up to 16,000) and throughput (up to 1,000 MB/s) independently from capacity, so you pay only for the performance you need rather than over-sizing the volume — the cost-effective choice here. st1 and sc1 are HDD types optimized for sequential throughput, not the steady random IOPS a database needs, and sc1 in particular targets infrequently accessed cold data. io2 would also meet the IOPS but at higher cost than gp3 for this moderate requirement.

questions.stem: To satisfy a disaster-recovery requirement, objects written to a primary S3 bucket in eu-west-1 must be automatically copied to a bucket in us-east-1. What configuration is required? (Choose two)
options: Use Same-Region Replication (SRR) between the two buckets
Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR) with an IAM role
Enable versioning on both the source and destination buckets
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the source bucket
questions.explanation: Correct: Cross-Region Replication copies objects to a bucket in a different region and requires versioning enabled on both source and destination plus an IAM role granting S3 replication permissions. Transfer Acceleration only speeds client uploads via edge locations and does not copy objects between buckets. SRR replicates within the same region, which does not meet a cross-region DR requirement. Note existing objects are not replicated unless you run S3 Batch Replication.
